title: Why writers delete the key instead of updating it
caption: Two writers that each SET the cache can finish in the opposite order to their database writes, leaving an old value that only the TTL will clear.

messages.label: UPDATE stock = 4
messages.note: Writer 2 commits second, so the database correctly holds 4.

messages.label: SET stock = 5
messages.note: Writer 1 was slow (GC pause, network) and its cache write lands last. The cache now says 5 while the database says 4.

messages.label: fix: DEL stock
messages.note: With delete-on-write both writers just remove the key, and the next read loads 4 from the database.

scenarios.name: Risk: DEL, then stale refill
scenarios.summary: Delete-on-write still has a rare race: a slow reader can put the old row back after the writer's DEL. The TTL bounds how long it lives.
scenarios.caption: Rare in practice (the reader must be slower than the whole write), so most systems accept it and rely on the TTL.

messages.label: miss → SELECT stock (5)
messages.note: A reader misses and reads the current value, 5.

messages.label: UPDATE stock = 4
messages.note: Before the reader fills the cache, a writer commits 4…

messages.label: DEL stock
messages.note: …and deletes the key, which isn't there yet.

messages.label: SET stock = 5 EX 300
messages.note: The reader's fill lands last: the cache holds the old 5 until the TTL.

messages.label: fix: delayed second DEL
messages.note: Mitigations: short TTL, a second DEL a moment later, or a versioned SET that refuses older versions.

scenarios.name: Invalidation lost
scenarios.summary: The database commits but the DEL never reaches the cache (crash, network blip). Without a TTL the stale value would live forever.

messages.label: DEL stock
messages.note: Writer 1 crashes, or the network drops the DEL.

messages.label: GET stock (old value)
messages.note: Readers keep getting the value from before the update.

messages.label: TTL expires → reload
messages.note: The TTL is the safety net: staleness is bounded by it. Retried or event-driven invalidation shrinks the window.

scenarios.name: Alternative: invalidate via CDC
scenarios.summary: Writers only write the database; a change-data-capture consumer reads the commit log and deletes keys, in commit order and with retries.
scenarios.caption: Invalidation becomes a pipeline driven by the database's own log instead of code in every writer.

messages.label: binlog: stock changed
messages.note: The change stream delivers every commit, in order.

messages.label: DEL stock
messages.note: The consumer deletes the key; if the cache is down, it retries from its log offset.

messages.label: lag ≈ 10–100 ms
messages.note: Trade-off: one more moving part, and a short window of staleness equal to the stream's lag.
